title: ABC Hydraulic Suspension System Leak

issues_found: DTC code C1402 is not a commonly cited Mercedes ABC-specific code; Mercedes typically uses proprietary codes like B4/5 pressure sensor codes for ABC faults
Upper repair cost bound of $6000 may be slightly low - full system overhauls can reach $7000-10000+
Not all listed models had ABC standard (S500/S550 was often optional); S600/CL600/AMG variants typically had it standard
audit.evidence: Multiple sources (RepairPal, MBWorld, Import-Car, independent shops) confirm ABC hydraulic leaks from struts, tandem pump, lines, and accumulators are a very common, well-documented issue on these vehicles, with the system operating at 3,000 PSI as stated. Repair costs cited in forums and shops range from ~$700 for a single strut to $5,000-$10,000+ for full system overhauls, broadly consistent with the listed range.

title: M272 Balance Shaft Gear Wear

issues_found: P0300 (random misfire) is not a typical DTC for this issue; P0016 and P0017 are the canonical codes
Year range 2005-2011 is too broad; affected production is primarily 2005 through late 2006/early 2007, with updated harder sprockets phased in by mid-2008
Severity 'high' may be overstated — issue is expensive but primarily a drivability/CEL problem, not safety-critical (medium would be more accurate)
Upper end of cost range slightly low; dealer repairs and some independent quotes range $5,500-$8,000
audit.evidence: The M272 balance shaft gear wear is a well-documented defect that was the subject of a U.S. class-action settlement (Seifi v. Mercedes-Benz USA, 2015) covering 2005-2007 M272 vehicles, caused by soft sprocket metal worn by the timing chain. Canonical fault codes are P0016/P0017 (camshaft correlation, right bank); typical independent repair runs ~$3,500 while dealer repairs exceed $5,500.

title: SAM Module Failure

issues_found: Solder joint cracking is less commonly cited than water intrusion/corrosion and flash memory wear as causes
DTC codes 'none' is acceptable but specific codes like B1048 can appear depending on which SAM circuit fails
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums (MBWorld, BenzWorld, MBClub UK) and specialist shops (MB Medic, Atlantic Motorcar, YouCanic) confirm SAM module failure is a common, well-documented issue on the W203 C-Class (2001-2007), typically caused by water intrusion/corrosion leading to erratic lights, wipers, and electrical malfunctions. Repair commonly requires module replacement plus SCN coding, fitting the $600-$1800 range.

title: M272 Balance Shaft Gear Wear and Failure

issues_found: Affected production range typically ends around 2007/2008 (engines built through October 2006 most affected); listing through 2010 likely overstates affected years
P0300 (misfire) is not a primary code for this issue—P0016/P0017 are the characteristic codes
Severity 'high' may be overstated; class-action and repair sources frame it as a costly reliability issue rather than safety-critical, though catastrophic engine damage is possible if ignored
Repair cost range starts low—typical independent shop repair is ~$3,500 and dealer/full repair can reach $6,000+
audit.evidence: Multiple sources (eEuroparts, MB Medic, Lone Star Bavarian, Import Performance, MBWorld forums) confirm the M272/M273 balance shaft/idler gear wear is a well-documented defect tied to a 2015 U.S. class-action settlement (Seifi v. MBUSA) covering 2005–2007 vehicles with affected engine serial numbers, with P0016/P0017 as the signature codes and typical repair costs of $3,500–$6,000.

title: AIRMATIC Air Suspension Compressor Failure

issues_found: DTC codes C1131/C1132 are level sensor fault codes (B22/8, B22/9), not compressor failure codes - compressor issues typically generate different codes
Year range starts at 2006, but the W221 S-Class generation began with model year 2007 in the US; 2006 was still W220 generation
Severity 'high' is arguable - vehicle is typically still drivable initially; 'medium' may be more appropriate as it's costly but not immediately safety-critical until full failure
Trim list mixes US and non-US trims (S350 was largely non-US for this generation)
audit.evidence: AIRMATIC compressor failure is a well-documented common issue on W221/W222 S-Class, often triggered by air spring/strut leaks causing the compressor to overwork, but the cited DTCs C1131/C1132 are documented as level sensor codes (C1132-C1135 range), not compressor failure codes. Repair cost range and general description are accurate, but the year range and DTC mapping are wrong.

title: Diesel Injector Failure and Black Death (OM651/OM654)

issues_found: Engine reference OM654 is questionable for US Sprinter year range; Black Death is most commonly associated with OM647/OM648 (T1N) and OM642 (V6), with OM651 also affected
DTC P0263 is a cylinder contribution code; Black Death typically presents visually or with misfire codes rather than specific injector circuit DTCs (P0201-P0204 are electrical injector circuit codes)
Sprinter 1500 trim did not exist until 2019 model year in the US market
Severity 'high' may be miscalibrated — per provided definitions this is 'costly but not dangerous' which fits 'medium' better, though external injector leaks can be a fire hazard
audit.evidence: Black Death is a widely documented, well-known Sprinter diesel issue where failed copper injector seal washers allow combustion gases to leak past the injector, creating hardened carbon deposits in the injector bore that can weld injectors in place. Repair shops cite costs from roughly $200 to $2900+ depending on severity, consistent with the entry's range.

title: ABC (Active Body Control) Hydraulic System Leak

issues_found: DTC codes C1301/C1401 not specifically verified as the standard codes for ABC hydraulic leaks; commonly cited codes include P1539 and B4/5 pressure sensor codes
Operating pressure of 3000 PSI is slightly high; one expert source cites ~2000 PSI generated by the ABC pump, though peak system pressures can approach ~200 bar
Upper bound of repair cost ($5000) may be conservative — full ABC overhauls/strut+pump+valve block jobs are frequently reported at $8000+
audit.evidence: ABC hydraulic leaks on the R230 SL are extensively documented across owner forums (MBWorld, MBClub UK), repair guides (BenzBits, YouCanic), RepairPal (248 reports for SL500), and NHTSA complaints, with leaks commonly occurring at valve blocks, struts, hoses, accumulators, and the tandem pump. Year range and model list match the R230 generation (2003-2012), and severity is appropriately rated high given documented cases of sudden suspension collapse while driving at highway speeds.

title: Air Suspension Failure (W212)

issues_found: AIRMATIC was an optional package on W212, not standard across all trims (especially uncommon on base E350); year range is broadly accurate but applies only to AIRMATIC-equipped cars

DTC C1132 could not be confirmed as the canonical code for this specific failure; commonly cited codes for W212 AIRMATIC faults include C1324/C1325 (rear axle damping valve unit) and level sensor codes
Severity 'high' is arguable - sagging/leak is a drivability and comfort issue rather than immediately safety-critical, though 'STOP VEHICLE TOO LOW' state can render car undriveable
Repair cost upper bound may be slightly low; full AIRMATIC repairs (multiple struts + compressor + valve block) can exceed $3000 at dealer
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums (MBWorld, MBClub UK, PistonHeads) and repair sites (MB Medic, Aerosus, AirSuspension.com) extensively document W212 AIRMATIC air spring leaks, compressor wear from overwork, and overnight sagging - exactly matching the described failure mode. However, the specific DTC C1132 is not corroborated as the typical code for this issue, and AIRMATIC was an optional package rather than standard on all listed trims.

title: AIRMATIC Air Suspension Strut and Compressor Failure

issues_found: DTC codes C1A20 and C1A13 do not appear in standard Mercedes AIRMATIC fault code lists; typical AIRMATIC codes for W164/W166 are in C1100-C1500 range (e.g., C1132, C1144, C1525)
AIRMATIC was an optional package on M-Class, not standard equipment - issue only applies to AIRMATIC-equipped vehicles
Severity 'high' is defensible (STOP VEHICLE TOO LOW warning can render car undrivable) but most failures are gradual sagging, not safety-critical
Repair cost range is reasonable but could skew higher - a single OEM strut at dealer can exceed $2,500
audit.evidence: Multiple sources (Suncore, MBWorld forums, Aerosus, MercedesMedic) confirm AIRMATIC air spring leaks and compressor failures are a well-documented issue on W164/W166 ML-Class, with air springs typically lasting 60-70k miles and RepairPal data showing single strut replacement over $2,500. However, the specific DTC codes C1A20 and C1A13 are not found in any Mercedes DTC reference for AIRMATIC; documented AIRMATIC codes use C11xx/C15xx format.

title: DEF/AdBlue SCR System Faults and Derate

issues_found: Sprinter 1500 designation is unusual/incorrect - Sprinter typically sold as 2500/3500/4500; the 1500 was only sold briefly (2019+) and not all listed years
Issue only applies to diesel (BlueTEC/OM642/OM651/OM654) Sprinters, not gasoline variants
DTC P249D is less commonly cited for this specific issue cluster than P20E8 or P204F, though it is a valid reductant-related code
5 mph derate is the final stage after a multi-stage progression (warnings, then 55 mph limit, then 5 mph or no-start), not the initial symptom
Repair cost range is reasonable but could exceed $3500 if SCR catalyst replacement is required
audit.evidence: Multiple sources confirm Sprinter diesel DEF/SCR system failures (dosing module, NOx sensors, DEF heater, crystallization) trigger derate/countdown modes; P20EE, P207F, and P2BAD are valid SCR-related DTCs frequently seen on Sprinters, with P20EE specifically documented on 2018-2022 Sprinters for SCR efficiency issues. The 5 mph limp mode is a real, documented end-stage derate strategy used by Mercedes on Sprinter diesels.

title: 7G-Tronic Transmission Valve Body Failure

issues_found: P2714 is a less typical code for this failure - more commonly cited codes are P0717/P0718 (turbine speed sensor) and P0722 (output speed sensor); P0700 is a generic transmission MIL code
Severity 'high' is debatable - limp mode is disabling but allows limp-home driving, could arguably be 'medium', though sudden loss of gears in traffic is a safety concern
audit.evidence: The 722.9 7G-Tronic conductor plate/valve body failure is extensively documented as one of the most common Mercedes transmission failures, affecting CLS 350/500/550/63 AMG from late 2004 onward, with VGS1 (2004-2007/2008) units having the highest failure rate. Repair costs from multiple sources (Circuit Board Medics, MB Medic, dealer quotes) consistently fall in the $1,800-$4,000 range, matching the entry's $1,500-$4,000 estimate.

title: AIRMATIC Air Suspension Compressor Failure

issues_found: DTC codes C1A20 and C1A13 could not be verified as standard Mercedes AIRMATIC compressor codes; Mercedes typically uses codes in the B1545/C1525 family or proprietary codes like 5051/5052 for AIRMATIC compressor faults
Repair cost range ($1200-$3000) is reasonable for compressor + related components but RepairPal shows compressor-only replacement averages $883-$965; full system repairs commonly reach $3,000-$3,500
Year range is broadly accurate but GL-Class spans two chassis (X164: 2007-2012, X166: 2013-2016) which have different compressor part numbers and slightly different failure characteristics
audit.evidence: Multiple sources (MBWorld forum, Strutmasters, Aerosus, mercedesassistance.com) confirm AIRMATIC compressor failure is a well-documented common issue on the GL-Class, with the root cause overwhelmingly cited as overwork from leaking air springs—matching the description exactly. Repair costs and severity align with industry data, but the specific DTC codes listed could not be independently verified.

title: Air Suspension Compressor Failure

issues_found: DTC codes C1131/C1132 are incorrect for compressor failure - C1132 is a level sensor fault code (component B22/8), not a compressor code. The C1132-C1135 range relates to ride height level sensors, not the compressor itself.
Issue only applies to GLE models optioned with AIRMATIC (Code 489) - not all GLE350/450/53/63 trims have air suspension; many ship with standard coil springs or E-Active Body Control

Severity 'high' is debatable - compressor failure typically causes ride degradation/sagging rather than immediate safety risk, though it can render vehicle undriveable in extreme cases (medium may be more appropriate)
Description claim that 'heavy SUV puts more stress on compressor than sedan applications' is plausible/anecdotal but not a formally documented engineering finding
audit.evidence: Multiple sources confirm AIRMATIC compressor failure is a well-known GLE issue, typically caused by overworking the compressor when air springs develop leaks. However, DTC C1132 is documented as a level sensor fault (B22/8), and the C1132-C1135 range pertains to ride height sensors rather than the compressor; correct compressor-related codes would typically be in different ranges (e.g., C1120-series for compressor/relay or pressure-related faults).

title: Turbo Resonator Crack and Boost Leak

issues_found: P0234 (overboost) is less commonly associated with this failure than P2359 or P2510; P0299 is the primary code and P0234 is plausible but secondary
Repair cost range is reasonable for DIY/independent shop but dealer pricing can exceed $600
audit.evidence: Multiple independent sources (Oregon Fuel Injection, Sprinter-Source forum, Turbochargers Direct, Go-Parts, Tactic Engineering, idparts) confirm the plastic turbo resonator on OM642-equipped 2007-2018 Sprinters is a well-known failure point that cracks/seal-fails from heat and vibration, causing boost leaks, P0299 underboost code, limp mode, and power loss especially under load. Aftermarket aluminum 'resonator delete' pipes are a common permanent fix, with part costs of $40-$150 plus labor aligning with the $200-$600 estimate.

title: AIRMATIC Air Suspension Failure

issues_found: DTC code C1132 is not clearly documented as an AIRMATIC-specific code for GLS; AIRMATIC fault codes are typically in different ranges and the source did not confirm C1132 maps to air spring/compressor failure
GLS63 AMG typically uses Active Body Control (ABC) or E-Active Body Control rather than standard AIRMATIC, so lumping it in with the others may be inaccurate
Year range spans two generations (X166: 2017-2019 and X167: 2020-2023); failure modes and parts differ between them but issue is documented in both
Claim that 'front air springs tend to fail first' is not strongly supported — multiple sources indicate rear air springs/struts are the more common failure point
audit.evidence: Multiple independent sources (RepairPal, Strutmasters, MB Medic, AirSuspension.com) confirm AIRMATIC air spring leaks and compressor burnout are common, well-documented failure modes on Mercedes GL/GLS vehicles, with RepairPal listing GLS450 air spring replacement at $885-$999 and compressor replacement at $1,301-$1,402, consistent with the stated $800-$4000 range. NHTSA campaign 20V-329 also covered some 2020 GLS450/GLS580 vehicles for defective strut piston seals, supporting the issue's reality.

title: Retractable Hardtop Hydraulic System Failure

issues_found: DTC field says 'none' but module-specific fault codes (e.g., microswitch S127/1, S119 faults) can be stored, though many hydraulic leaks produce no codes
Year range 2003-2020 is broadly correct but SL500 nameplate ended ~2006 in US (replaced by SL550); minor model-year/nameplate inconsistencies
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums (BenzWorld, MBWorld, Mercedes Club UK) and the specialist rebuilder Top Hydraulics extensively document Vario Roof failures on R230 (2003-2012) and R231 (2012-2020) SL-Class, including hydraulic cylinder seal leaks (top lock cylinder A230 800 08 72 typically first to fail), pump failures, and microswitch faults (S69, S118, S119, S126, S127). Repair costs documented range from ~$700-$900 for a single cylinder at independents up to $4,000-$5,000 for full system repair at dealers, matching the stated $800-$4000 range.

title: Glow Plug Failure and Cold Start Issues

issues_found: Sprinter 1500 trim didn't exist until 2019 model year - trim list mixes eras incorrectly
OM642 V6 was only offered roughly 2007-2018; 2019+ Sprinters primarily use 4-cylinder OM651/OM654, so 'OM642 V6 particularly prone' claim doesn't apply to entire 2007-2025 range
DTC P0670 is glow plug control module circuit (not always primary code on Sprinter); P0671 is cyl 1 - actual range used is typically P0671-P0676 for individual cylinders
Repair cost upper bound of $1500 may be low for worst-case scenarios requiring cylinder head removal (can exceed $3000-5000 per multiple shop reports)
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums, repair shops, and tool manufacturers confirm glow plug seizure/breakage in cylinder head is a well-documented Sprinter/OM642 issue, with DTCs P0380 and P0671-P0676 commonly reported. Symptoms (hard cold starts, white smoke, rough idle) and repair complexity match owner reports, though worst-case repairs requiring head removal can exceed the stated cost ceiling.

title: M272 Balance Shaft Sprocket Wear

issues_found: P0300 (misfire) is not a primary DTC for this issue; the characteristic codes are P0016 and P0017 (camshaft/crankshaft correlation), occasionally P0018/P0019
Repair cost range ($2000-$4500) is on the low end; independent shops typically quote ~$3,500 and dealers $5,500-$8,000+ since engine removal is often required

Severity 'high' is arguable per the rubric provided — this is a gradual wear issue with CEL warning, not a sudden safety-critical failure, so 'medium' (costly but not dangerous) fits the definitions better, though catastrophic engine damage is possible if ignored
Description says 'idler gear wears' but on the M272 V6 it is specifically the balance shaft sprocket that wears (the idler gear wear is the M273 V8 variant of the defect)
audit.evidence: Multiple sources (MB Medic, Import Performance, MBWorld forums, class-action lawsuit Seifi v. Mercedes-Benz USA settled 2015) confirm the M272 balance shaft sprocket defect affects 2006-2011 ML350 W164, with characteristic codes P0016/P0017 and repairs commonly $3,500 independent to $5,500-$8,000+ at dealer. The affected engine serial numbers concentrate in 2005-early 2007 production.

title: COMAND Head Unit Failure

issues_found: W221 S-Class uses NTG3 (2007-2009) and NTG3.5 (2009-2013), not NTG4 - NTG4 was used in other Mercedes models like the W204 C-Class
Description mentions 'internal hard drive' degradation, but NTG3/NTG3.5 head units use NAND flash memory and ICs/voltage regulators, not a spinning hard drive
DTC codes listed as 'none' is acceptable but D014/D015 MOST network voltage codes are commonly associated
audit.evidence: Multiple sources (MBWorld, BenzWorld, Module Medics, Braybrooks, ecudepot) confirm COMAND head unit failures are a well-known issue on 2007-2013 W221 S-Class with symptoms including black screen, no sound, and DVD/navigation failures. Repair specialists confirm failures stem from NAND memory, voltage regulators, defective ICs and board-level power faults on NTG3/NTG3.5 units (not NTG4), and repair/replacement costs in the $400-$3000 range are reasonable.

title: COMAND/MBUX Infotainment Freeze

issues_found: Severity arguably under-rated: NHTSA recall 21V354 classified the MBUX reboot issue as a safety concern because it could disable the rearview camera display, suggesting 'medium' may be more appropriate than 'low'
Description oversimplifies COMAND failure mode — owner reports point more to software/firmware bugs and head-unit hardware failures rather than specifically a 'hard drive' failure
MBUX issue is not primarily caused by 'connected phones' as described; the documented recall cause was MBUX software not meeting specifications, independent of phone connectivity
No DTCs listed is acceptable since issue is typically resolved via software update/recall rather than DTC-driven diagnostics
audit.evidence: NHTSA Recall 21V354 (Mercedes Campaign 2021080009) officially documents MBUX black-screen/reboot issues on 2019-2021 GLE and other models, fixed via dealer or OTA software update. Owner forums (MBWorld, BenzWorld, Mercedes GLE Forum) corroborate both COMAND freezes on pre-2020 GLE and MBUX reboot loops on 2020-2022 GLE, sometimes requiring head-unit replacement under warranty.

title: DCT Transmission Shudder

issues_found: Transmission misidentified as '8G-DCT' — the 2019-2023 A220 (W177) uses the 7G-DCT (7-speed dual-clutch), not an 8-speed

DTC P0725 (Engine Speed Input Circuit Malfunction) is not the appropriate code for DCT clutch shudder/judder; clutch-specific codes (P073x series) or manufacturer-specific transmission codes would be expected
Repair cost lower bound ($200) is optimistic; documented DCT repairs typically start higher, with clutch pack/mechatronic work running into thousands
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums (MBWorld, Edmunds long-term test) and repair sources confirm the 2019+ A220 W177 uses a 7-speed DCT and that jerky/shuddering low-speed shifts and clutch judder are widely reported, often addressed via TCU software updates or clutch component replacement. However, the entry's transmission designation (8G-DCT) is incorrect and P0725 is a generic engine-speed-sensor code rather than a DCT-shudder-specific DTC.

title: Significant Range Degradation in Cold Weather

issues_found: The claimed 30-40% cold weather range loss is at the high end of reported figures; most sources cite 20-30% as typical, with 30-35% only in worst-case highway/extreme cold scenarios

Description doesn't distinguish that early 2022-2023 EQS models lacked a standard heat pump (added for 2024 model year), which is the key reason early cars suffer more than the claimed 15-20% typical EV penalty
Statement that 'heat pump underperforms in extreme cold' is partially misleading for 2022-2023 models which generally did not have a heat pump at all
Issue is not a defect/TSB matter but an inherent EV characteristic, so 'no DTC codes' and 'low severity' are appropriately calibrated
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums (mbeqclub.com, mbworld.org) and EV publications confirm EQS owners report 25-35% winter range losses, with some extreme cases (-11°F to -13°F) reaching 40-50%. Notably, 2022-2023 EQS sedans shipped without a heat pump due to parts shortages; Mercedes added heat pumps standard for the 2024 model year to address cold-weather range complaints, meaning the year range is accurate but the root cause is more nuanced than described.

title: M271 Timing Chain Stretch and Tensioner Failure

issues_found: Year range starts at 2005 but R171 SLK with M271 began in 2004
Inclusion of 'SLC' is incorrect - SLC nameplate started 2016 (R172) and is not affected by this specific M271 issue in the same way
DTC P0341 is camshaft position sensor range/performance; P0017 (crank/cam correlation bank 1 sensor B) is more commonly cited alongside P0016 for this issue
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums (SLKWorld) and specialty sources confirm M271 timing chain stretch, tensioner failure, and worn camshaft adjuster sprockets causing startup rattle and potential engine damage; sources cite P0016/P0017 as typical DTCs and repair costs around €2000-€3000 including parts and labor.

title: 9G-Tronic Harsh Shift

issues_found: GLS580 nameplate did not exist until 2020 (X167 platform); 2017-2019 was GLS550 with 7G-Tronic, not 9G-Tronic — so model/year pairing for GLS580 is partly inaccurate

Description conflates general drivability complaints with the documented NHTSA recall 24V-118, which is specifically a 7-to-6 downshift TCU software defect causing engine stall (a safety issue), affecting only 6-cyl GLS 450 (not GLS 580)
No DTCs listed is plausible for software/adaptation issues, but TCU/mechatronics faults typically do log codes — 'none' may be incomplete

Severity 'medium' understates the related safety recall, which involves loss of propulsion (would be 'high' for the recall scope); 'medium' is fair only for non-recall harsh-shift drivability complaints
Repair cost range is plausible but software updates under recall are free; high end ($2500) only applies to out-of-warranty mechatronics/TCU replacement
audit.evidence: NHTSA Recall 24V-118 (Feb 2024) covers 2020-2023 GLE 450/GLS 450 6-cyl with 9-speed for TCU software causing potential engine stall during 7-to-6 downshift; owner forums (MBWorld) and independent shops document general 9G-Tronic harsh shift and hunting complaints across GLS models. GLS580 was not part of the transmission recall, and the 9G-Tronic harsh-shift behavior described is a separate, broader drivability concern.

title: Seat Control Module Failure

issues_found: DTC codes listed as 'none' but specific codes are well documented (9210 'System failure of backrest module carrier', 9211 'System failure of cushion module carrier', 9202 'module carrier for massage function', 9180/9181 pressure supply cut off, 9260 insufficient pressure supply)

Description misattributes root cause: the most common failure mode is the pneumatic system (leaking air bladders, cracked hoses, faulty valves in module carriers/pads, vacuum pump leaks), not the electronic control module itself; Mercedes TSB explicitly warns against replacing the control module/pump before checking pneumatic components

Claim that module is 'built into the seat frame and exposed to heat and vibration' is inaccurate - the seat control module is mounted in the seatback and is removable; the integrated valve/module carriers are in the cushion and backrest pads
Year range 2007-2017 is awkward - covers all of W221 (2007-2013) and partial W222 (2014-2020); should likely extend to 2020 to capture full W222 generation since the issue persists
Repair cost range may be low-end - full pneumatic repairs (pump, hoses, bladder/module carrier replacement) at a dealer often exceed $1200; module-only replacement fits the range
audit.evidence: NHTSA TSB MC-10166102 and multiple owner forums (MBWorld, BenzWorld, Pelican Parts) confirm multi-contour/dynamic seat failures are common on W221 and W222 S-Class, but the documented root cause is typically faulty valve transistors in the bladder module carriers and pneumatic leaks rather than the seat control module itself, and specific DTCs (9202, 9210, 9211, 9180, 9181, 9260) are well-established.

title: Real-World Range Significantly Below EPA Rating

issues_found: EPA range of 243 miles is only accurate for the EQB 250+ trim; the 300 4MATIC is rated ~205 miles and 350 4MATIC ~207 miles, so listing one EPA number for all three trims is misleading

Claim of '20-30% below EPA even in moderate weather' is overstated; independent tests (e.g., Edmunds) actually exceeded EPA on a 2023 EQB 350, and typical real-world is 70-85% of EPA (mostly highway-driven, not moderate-weather mixed)
Attributing aero inefficiency to the 'three-row layout' is misleading - the boxy shape is inherent to the GLB-based platform regardless of whether the optional third row is equipped
This is a characteristic/expectation gap rather than a defect; no TSBs, recalls, or DTCs apply - categorization as a known 'issue' is borderline
audit.evidence: Multiple sources confirm the EQB's boxy shape causes steep highway-range drops and real-world results typically land at 70-85% of EPA, particularly on AWD trims. However, the 243-mile EPA figure applies only to the 250+; the 4MATIC variants are EPA-rated around 205-207 miles, and at least one independent test (Edmunds) exceeded the EPA rating on mixed driving.

title: 8G-DCT Transmission Shudder

issues_found: Severity 'medium' may be slightly overstated - many reported cases are resolved by software updates/TSB flashes rather than mechanical repair, leaning toward low/nuisance
Description implies clutch pack wear as a common cause, but documented cases overwhelmingly point to software calibration issues fixed by dealer reflash; physical clutch failure is rare under 100k km
DTC codes listed as 'none' is plausible since many complaints are driveability-related without stored fault codes, though specific TSB references would strengthen the entry
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forum threads (MBWorld, GLA Owners) document 2021-2023 GLB250 owners reporting rough shifting, hesitation, and clunking at low speeds with the 8G-DCT, often resolved by a dealer software update/TSB reflash. Technical sources confirm the 724.1 8G-DCT does use wet multi-plate clutches as described, and clutch wear is documented as possible with aggressive driving.

title: 12V Auxiliary Battery Drain

issues_found: DTC U0100 (Lost Communication With ECM/PCM) is not the typical code for 12V battery drain; Mercedes uses energy management/battery-specific codes and warning messages like 'switch on vehicle to charge the 12V battery' rather than U0100
Repair cost range ($150-$500) may be low; forum reports indicate battery replacement alone runs ~$500-600 plus labor, and dealer diagnostics with the special charging device can push costs higher
The 7-10 day discharge window is anecdotal; actual drain times vary widely and many cases are tied to defective batteries or software bugs rather than guaranteed timing
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums (MBWorld, mbeqclub) and a Mercedes EQS-specific repair guide confirm widespread 12V auxiliary battery drain/failure issues on 2022+ EQS and EQE models, with Mercedes issuing software updates and a TSB on NHTSA addressing yellow 12V battery warning messages. However, the cited DTC U0100 is a generic communication-loss code not specifically tied to this symptom, and reported parts costs alone (~$500-600) suggest the upper cost bound is slightly understated.

title: Front Suspension Strut Noise

issues_found: Repair cost upper bound likely too low - RepairPal cites $1,380-$1,573 for full strut replacement, though strut mount only replacement can be cheaper
Description conflates two generations (C117 2014-2019 and C118 2020-2023) which have different suspension designs and aren't strictly the same platform issue
Most CLA-specific forum reports of clunking trace to ball joints/control arms or sway bar links rather than strut mount bearings specifically
Claim that CLA 'shares platform with A-Class' is only true for 2nd gen (C118/W177); 1st gen CLA (C117) shared platform with prior A-Class (W176)
audit.evidence: Front suspension noise (clunking/creaking) is widely documented for the CLA across both generations, with strut mounts/bearings cited as one cause alongside ball joints and sway bar links. RepairPal lists strut replacement at $1,380-$1,573, exceeding the stated $200-$1,000 cost range, though isolated strut mount/bearing replacement can fall within range.

title: MBUX Infotainment System Freeze

issues_found: DTC codes field is 'none' which is accurate for this software-related issue, though some forum reports mention head unit replacement costs that could exceed $2000 (up to ~$6000 CAD / 1800 euro)
Repair cost upper bound may be slightly low if full head unit replacement is needed out of warranty
audit.evidence: <cite index="10-2,10-3">NHTSA Recall 21V354 confirmed MBUX software issues on 2019-2021 GLC-Class (253 platform) vehicles where the multimedia system might not start, display might remain black, or reboot unintentionally after 50 seconds of startup</cite>. <cite index="18-3,18-4">A more recent recall affects 2024-2026 GLC-Class and other models where the control unit triggers system resets causing display interruptions</cite>, and <cite index="14-3">Bluetooth, Apple CarPlay, and Android Auto disconnect issues are common software-related complaints on MBUX</cite>.

title: Dual-Clutch Transmission (DCT) Shudder at Low Speeds

issues_found: B250e (electric variant) does not use the 7G-DCT transmission — it has a single-speed reduction gear, so including B250e in the affected models is incorrect

Mercedes diagnostic sources confirm 12V undervoltage on modern MBs commonly triggers cascading module communication faults (e.g., LIN-bus codes like B11DB87) and battery replacement costs in the $250–$450+ range, consistent with the entry.

title: Convertible Soft-Top Alignment, Latch, and Water Leak Problems on R232 Roadsters

issues_found: Specific documented evidence of widespread R232 soft-top alignment/latch/leak complaints is limited compared to older SL generations; most forum reports concern R129/R230/R231
DTC codes are vague ('latch module faults may be stored') rather than specific codes
SL43 was not available from 2022 - it was added in 2023, so the year range for SL43 is slightly off
Repair cost upper bound ($2500) may be optimistic if full roof mechanism work is needed at a Mercedes dealer
audit.evidence: Mercedes-Benz publishes an official 'Problems with the soft top' section in the R232 owner's manual confirming soft-top troubleshooting is a recognized topic, and CarGurus notes 2022+ R232 SLs are known for electrical gremlins attributed to rushed production. However, specific high-volume complaints about R232 alignment, latching, and water leaks are less documented than for prior SL generations; the SL43 also wasn't introduced until 2023.

title: Front Brake Squeal and Premature Rotor/Pads Wear on AMG Performance Brake Packages

issues_found: Brake squeal is a well-documented characteristic of AMG high-performance semi-metallic brakes across the entire AMG lineup, not a defect specific to the R232 SL-Class
No specific NHTSA complaints or TSBs found uniquely tying premature rotor/pad wear to the 2022-2025 SL 55/63 - evidence is largely extrapolated from other AMG models (C63, E63, GLA35, etc.)
Mercedes/AMG officially considers the squeal 'normal and expected' rather than a defect requiring repair, which may make the medium severity slightly overstated for the noise component
Repair cost ceiling of $2,200 may be low; AMG front brake jobs (especially with rotors) at dealers have been reported at $2,500-$4,100+
No DTC codes is correct (brake noise/wear typically does not set codes)
audit.evidence: Multiple owner forums and Mercedes dealer service pages confirm AMG performance brakes commonly squeal due to semi-metallic pad compounds, with the manufacturer position being that it is normal behavior rather than a defect. However, evidence specifically tied to the 2022-2025 R232 SL 55/63 is thin - most documented complaints come from other AMG models (C63, E63, GLA35 AMG, E53), suggesting the issue is generalized to AMG brakes rather than an SL-specific known issue.

title: Rear-Axle Steering Control Unit/Software Fault Causing Warning Messages and Reduced Stability Functions

issues_found: Year range overstated: documented service campaign 2023030017 covers MY 2022-2023 only, not through 2025
Severity 'high' is likely overstated - Mercedes stated vehicle remains operational and safe to drive when the fault message appears
Repair cost range ($0-$3500) is misleading - the remedy is a free dealer software update under service campaign, not a paid repair
DTC reference is vague; documented related fault codes include C112502 in the rear axle steering control unit (N68/4), which the entry does not specify
Described as a 'recall' but it is actually a Mercedes service campaign (22P5496211 / MBUSA 2023030017), not a formal NHTSA safety recall
audit.evidence: Mercedes-Benz issued Service Campaign 2023030017 (22P5496211) in April 2023 for approximately 1,365 MY2022-2023 R232 SL vehicles to update the left and right rear axle steering control unit software, because a rear axle steering fault message could sporadically appear in the instrument cluster at engine start; MBAG explicitly noted the vehicle remains operational and safe to drive. NHTSA TSBs also document related rear-axle-steering fault messages and fault code C112502 in control unit N68/4 on the R232 platform.

title: Battery Voltage and Electronic Module Faults

issues_found: DTC codes U0121 (ABS module communication) and U0140 (Body Control Module communication) are generic codes not specifically tied to Mercedes battery/auxiliary battery faults; Mercedes typically stores B-codes like B1D13, B212D, or B21DC01 in the Energy Management/EIS module for these symptoms
P0562 (system voltage low) is appropriately listed
Repair cost range is reasonable but could extend higher if both main and auxiliary batteries need replacement plus registration/coding
audit.evidence: Multiple Mercedes-specific sources confirm that SLC and related models are highly sensitive to weak main/auxiliary battery voltage, triggering start-stop malfunctions, dashboard warnings, comfort feature shutoffs, and erratic module behavior; a JustAnswer case specifically involves a 2018 SLC 300 with battery-related dashboard warnings after battery replacement, and Mercedes' battery management system is documented to switch off consumers in priority stages when voltage drops. However, the U-series DTCs listed are generic CAN-bus codes not typically associated with this specific battery-voltage symptom pattern in Mercedes diagnostics.

title: Crankcase Ventilation / PCV Valve Failure

issues_found: DTC codes are incorrect - actual documented code is P052E/P052E71 (Positive Crankcase Ventilation Regulator Valve Performance), not P0171/P0507/P2187
Repair cost range is low - real-world dealer repairs commonly run $1200-$2500+, with the upper bound of $1100 below typical dealer pricing
Description mentions 'lean-mixture faults' which is not the primary documented symptom; CEL with P052E71 is the hallmark
audit.evidence: NHTSA TSB MC-11013091-0001 and MBUSA extended warranty NCU (MC-10241531-0001) explicitly document the partial-load crankcase ventilation valve / intake line assembly failure on SLK/SLC300 and other M274-equipped vehicles, with fault code P052E71 as the diagnostic identifier; MBUSA extended emissions warranty to 15 years/150,000 miles. Owner forums (MBWorld, BenzWorld, Metris, GLC) confirm widespread failures with typical dealer repair costs of $1,200-$2,500.

title: Balance Shaft Sprocket Wear

issues_found: DTC list includes P1200 which is not a standard code for this issue - the '1200' referenced in Mercedes diagnostics is an internal MB code that maps to P0017, not OBD-II P1200
P0018/P0019 (Bank 2 correlation codes) are less commonly reported - the documented failure primarily affects the right cylinder bank producing P0016/P0017

Severity rated 'high' is debatable - per the definition provided, this is a costly repair but not directly safety-critical (rough running/stalling could be argued as safety-relevant in severe cases), 'medium' may be better calibrated

Year range is reasonable but the affected range is more precisely tied to engine serial numbers up to 2729..30 468993, with most failures in 2005-2007 production; 2008 cars are often outside the affected serial range
audit.evidence: Multiple independent sources (Mercedes TSB S-B-03.30/08i, a 2015 U.S. class-action settlement covering 2005-2007 M272/M273 vehicles with extended coverage to 10yr/125k miles, and numerous owner forum reports) confirm premature balance shaft sprocket wear on M272 V6 engines causing P0016/P0017 cam-crank correlation codes. Repair costs of $3,500 at independent shops to $5,500+ at dealers align with the stated $3,500-$6,500 range.
